## Question:

Is attending a more expensive college associated with higher earnings after college, and is this relationship different for public and private universities?

## The Data

This is the college scorecard data, publicly available on data.gov. I am using the latest update, noted to be November 2 2026 (accessed November 6 2026).

## The why

College is becoming increasingly expensive at an alarming rate. For many, it has simply become too much and is written off as a bad investment. For others, even if they see it as a good investment they may find that the debt is crippling. I want to explore this dilemma by answering which undergraduate institutions have the best ROI and provide insight to those who see university education as a risky investment.

## Variables

Average annual net price: NPT4_PUB (Public schools) \| Quantitative

NPT4_PRIV (Private schools) \| Quantitative

NOTE: these net prices are collected based on students who received federal aid, so this is not an entirely representative number.

Median earnings 10 years after entry: MD_EARN_WNE_P10 \| Quantitative

Institution type: CONTROL \| Categorical \| Private == 2 , Public == 1

Institution name: INSTNM \| Identifier \|

Predominant Degree: PREDDEG (bachelors == 3) \| Identifier

## Packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse) #using readr, dyplr, ggplot2 from tidyverse
```

## Reading the Data

```{r}
College_Data = read_csv('Most-Recent-Cohorts-Institution.csv', col_names=TRUE)
College_Data = College_Data %>%
  rename(Institution_Name = 'INSTNM',
         Institution_Type = 'CONTROL',
         Predominant_Degree = 'PREDDEG',
         Avg_Ann_Net_Price_Public = 'NPT4_PUB',
         Avg_Ann_Net_Price_Private = 'NPT4_PRIV',
         Median_Earn_10_Years = 'MD_EARN_WNE_P10') %>%
  filter(Predominant_Degree == 3,
         Institution_Type == 1 | Institution_Type == 2,
         !(is.na(Avg_Ann_Net_Price_Public) & is.na(Avg_Ann_Net_Price_Private)),
         Median_Earn_10_Years != 'PS' & Median_Earn_10_Years != 'NULL') %>% 
# Filters to only bachelors degrees, public and private schools, removes rows with na values in both public and private price, and removes rows with private earnings data and Null data
  mutate(Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General = if_else(is.na(Avg_Ann_Net_Price_Public),  Avg_Ann_Net_Price_Private, Avg_Ann_Net_Price_Public),
         Median_Earn_10_Years = as.numeric(Median_Earn_10_Years),
         Institution_Type = if_else(Institution_Type == 1, 'Public', 'Private')) %>%
# creates a general price column that includes no NA values for all institutions. Then I convert median earnings column to numeric as it was in character. Then I make institution type column more descriptive.
  select(Institution_Name,
         Institution_Type,
         Avg_Ann_Net_Price_Public,
         Avg_Ann_Net_Price_Private,
         Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General,
         Median_Earn_10_Years) 
# only selecting the variables that I will use for this project
```

```{r}
table(College_Data$Institution_Type)
```

-We have 1025 Private Colleges and 565 Public Colleges in our Data

## Figure 1 - Scatterplot, Linear Model, Limitations

Scatter plot with average annual price on the x axis and median earnings after 10 years on the y axis. Colored by public or private. Includes a linear model for both institution types.

```{r}
ggplot(College_Data, aes(x=Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General, y=Median_Earn_10_Years, color = Institution_Type, fill = Institution_Type)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, shape = 24) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Price vs Earnings by Public or Private Universities", x = "Average Annual Net Price", y = "Median Earnings after 10 Years", color = "Public or Private?", fill = "Public or Private?") 
```

At lower price, public schools appear to beat out private schools in earnings. However, all high earning outlier instututions are private. Notably, the 3 schools that have earnings above \$150,000 are MIT, Harvey Mudd, and Cal Tech. While these schools do have high educational reputation, one thing I notice is that all three are strictly STEM-focused in program offerings. Therefore, reputation and educational prowess may not be the lone reason for high earnings numbers. I wanted to go further in this idea so I looked at the bottom 3 institutions in earnings: Talmudical Seminary of Bobov, Yeshivath Viznitz, and Universidad Teologica del Caribe. The Talmudical Seminary of Bobov and Yeshivath Viznitz are Jewish institutions offering only degree programs in Rabbinical studies, Jewish history, and similar. These programs may not generally offer the same level of financial wellness as a tech degree.

In conclusion, the degree plans offered (only STEM, religious studies) may impact earning numbers, a limitation in the data.

The most expensive public school tops out at \$35957, well below that of many private schools. This is a limitation I can handle. As to only compare values within the same interval of price, I will cap the private institutions at \$35957 in average net price.

## Figure 2 - Capped Price on Private Institutions

```{r}
College_Data %>%
  filter(Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General <= 35957) %>%
#filter out colleges exceeding that price
  ggplot(aes(x=Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General, y=Median_Earn_10_Years, color =              Institution_Type, fill = Institution_Type)) +
    geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, shape = 24) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    theme_bw() +
    labs(title = "Price vs Earnings by Public or Private Universities", x = "Average Annual Net Price", y = "Median Earnings after 10 Years", color = "Public or Private?", fill = "Public or Private?") 
```

That is better, the lines look similar, however it appears the linear models ever-so-slightly got farther from each other at lower prices and closer at higher prices. At a price tag of \$30,000, there is almost no observed significant difference between institution types. I'll use this filtered data for the next figure.

## Summary/Hypothesis Test - Linear Regression with Interaction

```{r}
College_Data_Updated = College_Data %>%
  filter(Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General <= 35957)

fit = lm(Median_Earn_10_Years ~ Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General * Institution_Type, data = College_Data_Updated)
summary(fit)
```

This gives us the equations of our two lines. It is also important to note that the investment of college is typically over the course of 4 years. In other words, Average annual price \* 4.

"ROI" Estimate: I will calculate a number that shows the % of the full investment of college that is paid per-year, 10 years later.

"ROI" Estimate: Earnings ÷ 4 \* Average Annual Net Price.

It is important to note that with an R squared of about 0.12, we can only say that about 12% of the variation in earnings is actually attributed to the factors explored in this data, so while a relationship does exist, it must be taken with a grain of salt.

Just so that I can say the separate linear model is significant for both public and private institutions, I will run another model with public as the baseline.

```{r}
fit_public = lm(Median_Earn_10_Years ~ Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General *
                  relevel(factor(Institution_Type), ref = "Public"), 
                #relevel is a function that tells R not to automatically select Private as the baseline for the regression.
                data = College_Data_Updated)
summary(fit_public)
```

I can conclude that public institutions have a positive slope in price vs earnings (p = 2.56e-06).

### Public Institutions

Starts at \$52,380, and after every \$1 spent per year, earnings go up by 56.4 cents (\$0.564) per year.

```{r}
Price = 20000
Annual_Earnings_Estimate_Public = 52380 + (0.564)*Price
Annual_Earnings_Estimate_Public
ROI_Estimate_Public = (52380 + (0.564)*Price) / (4 * Price)
ROI_Estimate_Public
```

Put a price in the code and get your estimates. For example, at \$20,000 spent per year, you are estimated to earn \$63,660 per year, 10 years after. That would mean you are making back 79.6% of your \$80,000 total investment into college, yearly.

### Private Institutions

Starts at \$37,700, and after every \$1 spent per year, earnings go up by \$1.01

```{r}
Price = 20000
Annual_Earnings_Estimate_Private = 37700 + (1.01)*Price
Annual_Earnings_Estimate_Private
ROI_Estimate_Private= (37700 + (1.01)*Price) / (4*Price)
ROI_Estimate_Private
```

Put a price in the code and get your estimates. For example, at \$20,000 spent per year, you are estimated to earn \$57,900 per year, 10 years after. That would mean you are making back 72.4% of your \$80,000 total investment into college, yearly.

### Observation

- The slope of the Private institution estimator is \$1.01, I find it really cool that it is so close to just being \$1. I wonder if there is a good reason for that or if this is coincidence. A hypothesis of mine would be the possibility of for-profit private institutions optimizing their price for higher earnings.

- The price vs earnings relationship (p = 0.0016) is significantly different for public and private institutions.

## Hypothesis Test - Are Public and Private Earnings different at a typical price?

```{r}
Median_Price = median(College_Data_Updated$Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General)
Median_Price
```

The median price across both types is \$19090. I will use this as a 'typical' price to test whether earnings predictions differ between public and private institutions. Since the last regression tested a significant difference at \$0, I will subtract \$19090 from each observation of the prices and so we will be testing the difference at that median number.

```{r}
College_Median = College_Data_Updated %>%
  mutate(Price_Vs_Median = Avg_Ann_Net_Price_General - Median_Price)
fit = lm(Median_Earn_10_Years ~ Price_Vs_Median * Institution_Type, data = College_Median)
summary(fit)
confint(fit)
```

It is statistically significant that public institutions earn more money than private institutions at the median price (p= 1.97e-09)!

With 95% confidence, I can suggest that the difference in earnings at this price is estimated between \$4156 and \$8156, in favor of public institutions.

## Conclusion

#### Q: Is attending a more expensive college associated with higher earnings after college, and is this relationship different for public and private universities?

Yes, attending a more expensive college has evidence of association with higher earnings, and this relationship differs for public and private institutions.

- Higher price is associated with higher earnings at private schools (p = 2 \* 10^-16^)

- Higher price is associated with higher earnings at public schools (p = 2.56 \* 10\^-6).

- It is estimated that at a private institution, for every \$1 spent, an additional \$1.01 is earned.

- At a public school, it is estimated that for every \$1 spent, an additional \$0.564 is earned.

- If one spent \$20,000 a year on a public school, it is estimated that 10 years later their yearly salary would be 79.6% of their total investment.

- If one spent \$20,000 a year on a private school, it is estimated that 10 years later their yearly salary would be 72.4% of their total investment.

- At the median college price of \$19,090, public institutions are found to earn more money than private institutions (p = 1.97 \* 10\^-10)

- The relationship of price vs earnings is different for public and private institutions (p = 0.0016).

- R-squared = \~0.12, which means only about 12% of the variation earnings actually boils down to public vs private.

- One found limitation is that some institutions specialize in degree programs that may typically have more lucrative careers, like those in STEM.
